chunks: Rules of thumb for routing high-speed signals. The question: What are some rules of thumb when routing high-speed signals?
A fast signal on a circuit board travels down the trace like a wave.
It stays clean only if the path keeps the same shape the whole way and the return current has a smooth path back.
Every routing rule protects one of those two things: a solid plane underneath, one trace width, few vias, no dead-end branches, and space from neighbors.
Imagine a ball rolling down a smooth, even gutter. It arrives cleanly. Add a gap, a narrow spot or a side branch, and part of its motion bounces back.
Fast signals do the same at every bump. What matters is how fast the edge is, not how often the signal repeats.
Below the line a trace may be treated as a wire; above it, as a transmission line that needs controlled impedance and probably termination.
Modern 100 picoseconds edges push the threshold to a few millimetres, which is why almost every trace on a fast board is "a transmission line".
Rise time ( t r ): how long a signal takes to go from low to high.
Transmission line: a trace long enough, compared with the edge, that the signal must be treated as a wave ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the ratio of voltage to current the wave sees, set by trace width, height above the plane and board material.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source. At high speed it is the plane right under the trace ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Stub: a dead-end branch that reflects part of the signal. Crosstalk: unwanted coupling from a neighboring trace.
A signal edge takes 1 nanoseconds to rise. On ordinary board material it travels about 5. 9 picoseconds per millimeter.
A trace counts as a transmission line when its one-way delay is more than about t r over 6 , here about 167 picoseconds. That is a critical length of 167 over 5. 9 about 28 mm.
Longer traces need the full set of rules. That is the whole idea.
"High-speed routing is about keeping the trace a uniform transmission line with a clean return path.

I route on a solid reference plane without crossing splits, keep one width for controlled impedance, avoid stubs, minimise vias and put a ground via beside each signal via, use 45° bends, keep about three trace widths of spacing, match lengths on buses and pairs, and terminate if the trace is long compared with the edge.
What counts is rise time, not clock frequency: if the one-way delay is more than a sixth of the rise time, it's a transmission line."
